items.definition: Educational philosophy advocating traditional basic skills (3Rs: Reading, 'Riting, 'Rithmetic) and core academic subjects taught through direct, teacher-centered instruction and rigorous discipline.
items.rationalization: Founded by William Bagley, Essentialism holds that schools should instill common cultural heritage, core knowledge, and hard work to prepare students to be contributing citizens.
items.source: PRC-BPT TOS Domain 1 (Foundations of Education); Bilbao, P. et al., The Teaching Profession (4th ed.), Ch. 1
items.tosCompetency: Analyze educational philosophies and their institutional applications

items.definition: Educational philosophy asserting that human nature is unchanging and education should focus on eternal, universal truths through the study of the Great Books and classic humanities.
items.rationalization: Championed by Robert Maynard Hutchins and Mortimer Adler, Perennialism cultivates rational intellect by engaging with timeless ideas that have stood the test of centuries.
items.source: PRC-BPT TOS Domain 1; Corpuz & Salandanan, Principles of Teaching 1, Ch. 2
items.tosCompetency: Distinguish classical educational philosophies in contemporary schooling

mnemonic.title: Perennialism Key
mnemonic.phrase: Perennial = Plants That Last Forever (Great Books)

items.definition: Philosophy promoting experiential 'learning by doing', democratic classrooms, problem-solving, and child-centered curricula based on students' real-life needs and interests.
items.rationalization: Founded by John Dewey, Progressivism rejects rote memorization in favor of hands-on projects, group cooperation, and scientific inquiry reflecting society.
items.source: PRC-BPT TOS Domain 1; John Dewey, Democracy and Education (1916)
items.tosCompetency: Apply student-centered educational theories to classroom instructional design

items.definition: Philosophy stressing individual freedom, personal choice, authentic self-definition, and accepting the moral responsibility of one's decisions without predefined societal scripts.
items.rationalization: Influenced by Jean-Paul Sartre and Soren Kierkegaard ('existence precedes essence'). In education, it allows students to choose their own learning paths and self-paced projects.

items.definition: Philosophy that views schools as catalysts and agents for social change, equipping students to critically address societal crises like poverty, injustice, and environmental damage.
items.rationalization: Led by George Counts and Theodore Brameld, it urges teachers and schools to lead community reconstruction rather than merely transmitting the existing social status quo.

items.definition: Educational approach developed by Paulo Freire that awakens critical consciousness ('conscientização') in students to challenge oppression and transform social structures.
items.rationalization: Freire condemned the 'banking concept of education' where teachers deposit knowledge into passive learners, advocating instead 'problem-posing' dialogical education.

items.definition: Psychological philosophy asserting that learning is a measurable change in observable behavior shaped by environmental stimuli, conditioning, and reinforcement schedules.
items.rationalization: Associated with B.F. Skinner, John B. Watson, and Ivan Pavlov. Uses positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, and drills to mold student habits.

items.definition: Learning theory positing that learners actively construct new knowledge and personal meaning from their experiences rather than passively receiving information.
items.rationalization: Pioneered by Jean Piaget (cognitive constructivism) and Lev Vygotsky (social constructivism). Emphasizes prior knowledge, scaffolding, discovery, and reflection.

items.definition: Philosophy originating with Plato holding that reality consists of spiritual ideas and unchanging mental constructs rather than physical matter.
items.rationalization: Idealist education emphasizes character development, intellectual contemplation, moral ideals, and the Socratic method to draw out innate truths from the soul.

items.definition: Philosophy founded by Aristotle asserting that reality exists independently of human minds and can be discovered objectively through sensory perception and the scientific method.
items.rationalization: Realist classrooms emphasize natural sciences, objective facts, lab experiments, categorization, and observable natural laws.

mnemonic.title: Realism Fact
mnemonic.phrase: Realism = Real World Outside the Mind

items.definition: Philosophy founded by Charles Sanders Peirce and William James asserting that the meaning and truth of an idea lies in its practical consequences and working utility.
items.rationalization: 'If it works in practice, it is true.' Pragmatism provided the foundational epistemology for Dewey's progressive education.

items.definition: Ethical philosophy formulated by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill stating that the moral worth of an action is determined by producing the greatest happiness for the greatest number.
items.rationalization: In education and school policy, utilitarian decisions prioritize programs and resource allocations that benefit the maximum majority of learners.

items.definition: Medieval philosophical approach synthesized by St. Thomas Aquinas that harmonizes Christian religious revelation with Aristotelian rational philosophy.
items.rationalization: Employs dialectical reasoning and disputation to prove that faith and human reason are complementary gifts of God (Thomism).

items.definition: Philosophical doctrine holding that pleasure is the ultimate good and pain is the principal evil, warning in its refined Epicurean form against excess.
items.rationalization: In education, teachers must avoid purely hedonistic short-term gratification, channeling natural interests toward long-term intellectual joy.

items.definition: Ancient Hellenistic philosophy teaching emotional self-control, acceptance of universal fate, endurance of hardship, and strict adherence to moral duty.
items.rationalization: Championed by Epictetus, Seneca, and Marcus Aurelius. Trains teachers and students to cultivate inner tranquility and focus only on what is within their control.

items.definition: Educational orientation rooted in Maslow and Carl Rogers emphasizing the whole child, affective emotional growth, self-actualization, and empathetic teacher-student rapport.
items.rationalization: Humanistic educators maintain that basic emotional and safety needs must be met before optimal cognitive learning and self-fulfillment can take place.

items.definition: Epistemological view stating that reason, deduction, and innate intellect are the primary sources of knowledge, rather than sensory experience.
items.rationalization: Founded by Rene Descartes ('Cogito, ergo sum'). Promotes mathematical deductive proofs, logic syllogisms, and rigorous mental deduction.

items.definition: Epistemological doctrine asserting that all knowledge originates solely through sensory experience and inductive observation of the external world.
items.rationalization: John Locke formulated the human mind as a 'tabula rasa' (blank tablet) waiting to be inscribed by sensations and reflection.

items.definition: Philosophical system created by Auguste Comte stating that authentic knowledge is strictly limited to verifiable scientific facts and empirical data.
items.rationalization: Positivism rejects religious dogma and metaphysical speculation, insisting that curriculum be rooted in objective, measurable scientific evidence.

items.definition: Educational philosophy of Jean-Jacques Rousseau asserting that human nature is inherently good and children should unfold according to natural developmental stages without artificial societal corruption.
items.rationalization: Detailed in Rousseau's masterpiece 'Emile', advocating education in harmony with nature and sensory exploration before formal book learning.

items.definition: The professional pedagogical approach of selecting, combining, and synthesizing best elements from different philosophies to fit the diverse needs of learners.
items.rationalization: Modern professional teachers in the Philippines are expected to be eclectic—employing direct instruction for basic phonics (essentialist) and group inquiry for science projects (progressivist).

items.definition: The major branch of philosophy that investigates the nature, sources, validity, and limitations of human knowledge ('How do we know what is true?').
items.rationalization: Epistemology shapes curriculum design and teaching methods by defining whether truth is discovered through reason, revelation, or sensory experiments.

items.definition: The branch of philosophy concerned with the fundamental nature of ultimate reality, being, and the universe ('What is real?').
items.rationalization: A teacher's metaphysical outlook determines whether their classroom prioritizes spiritual values (idealism) or physical physical facts (realism).

items.definition: The branch of philosophy that studies values and valuation, divided into Ethics (moral values) and Aesthetics (beauty and artistic taste).
items.rationalization: Axiology guides teachers in instilling moral character, civic values, and aesthetic appreciation in Philippine basic education.

items.definition: The subdivision of axiology that examines moral principles, right versus wrong conduct, and duties governing professional human behavior.
items.rationalization: Codified for Filipino teachers under the Code of Ethics for Professional Teachers (Resolution No. 435, s. 1997).

items.definition: The subdivision of axiology investigating criteria for beauty, artistic taste, expression, and the emotional impact of fine arts.
items.rationalization: Aesthetic education enriches MAPEH (Music, Arts, PE, Health) in Philippine curricula to foster cultural identity and creative imagination.

items.definition: The branch of philosophy that investigates the principles of correct reasoning, formal arguments, and valid inference.
items.rationalization: Divided into deductive logic (from general premise to specific conclusion) and inductive logic (from specific observations to general principle).

items.definition: A pedagogical technique of disciplined questioning (elenchus) that stimulates critical thinking and illuminates underlying presuppositions to deliver truth.
items.rationalization: Socrates compared himself to a midwife assisting the birth of innate ideas already slumbering inside the learner's mind.

items.definition: Paulo Freire's critical metaphor describing traditional classrooms where teachers deposit knowledge into passive student receptacles who merely receive and memorize.
items.rationalization: Freire advocated replacing banking education with problem-posing dialogue where teachers and students become co-investigators of reality.

items.definition: John Locke's Latin philosophical metaphor meaning 'blank slate', proposing that humans are born without innate ideas and acquire all knowledge through experience.
items.rationalization: Underpins the behaviorist and empiricist belief that a student's environment and education exert decisive influence over their development.

items.definition: Curricular model formulated by Robert Hutchins and Mortimer Adler basing higher education on reading foundational classical works across literature, philosophy, and science.
items.rationalization: A signature perennialist curriculum designed to discipline the intellect by dialoguing with humanity's greatest minds.

items.definition: Instructional support structure provided by a teacher or more capable peer that is gradually dismantled as the learner attains independent competence.
items.rationalization: Formulated by Jerome Bruner in conjunction with Lev Vygotsky's socio-cultural theory of cognitive development.

mnemonic.title: Scaffolding Bridge
mnemonic.phrase: Support Built Up, Then Taken Down

items.definition: The dynamic cognitive distance between what a learner can achieve independently and what they can achieve with guidance from a More Knowledgeable Other (MKO).
items.rationalization: Formulated by Lev Vygotsky; effective instruction targets tasks precisely within the learner's ZPD rather than tasks that are too easy or frustratingly difficult.

items.definition: Behavioral learning process developed by B.F. Skinner in which voluntary behaviors are strengthened or weakened through consequences such as reinforcement or punishment.
items.rationalization: Positive reinforcement increases behavior frequency by presenting pleasant stimuli; negative reinforcement increases behavior frequency by removing aversive stimuli.

items.definition: The mental state of balance achieved through assimilation (fitting new information into existing schemas) and accommodation (modifying existing schemas to fit new experiences).
items.rationalization: Jean Piaget highlighted that cognitive growth occurs when new experiences cause disequilibrium, spurring learners to adapt their mental schemas.

items.term: Code of Ethics for Professional Teachers (Article III)
items.definition: Mandates that teachers are facilitators of learning and official trustees of the cultural and educational heritage of the nation within community life.
items.rationalization: Article III obligates teachers to actively participate in community betterment, study local customs, and maintain honorable social standing.

items.definition: The modern progressive and constructivist metaphor contrasting with 'Sage on the Stage', portraying the teacher as coach, resource provider, and mentor.
items.rationalization: Promotes active student ownership of learning outcomes rather than unilateral teacher lecture monopolies.

mnemonic.title: Teacher Role Contrast
mnemonic.phrase: Guide on Side vs Sage on Stage

items.definition: Curricular organization rooted in developmental psychology and progressivism that places the child's readiness, interests, and developmental milestones at the focal point.
items.rationalization: Replaces rigid subject-matter silos with integrated thematic units and practical problem-solving tailored to the student's developmental stage.

mnemonic.title: Child-Centered Priority
mnemonic.phrase: Teach the Child, Not Just the Book

items.definition: Delors Report framework for 21st-century holistic education: Learning to Know, Learning to Do, Learning to Live Together, and Learning to Be.
items.rationalization: Learning to Live Together emphasizes empathy, peace, and mutual understanding; Learning to Be emphasizes full self-actualization of mind, body, and spirit.

mnemonic.title: UNESCO Pillars
mnemonic.phrase: K-D-LT-B: Know, Do, Live Together, Be
